Senses.Explanation: The graphs mean “receive or take up” and “bear or take charge of”: “to take on.” The dominant collocation is “take it on directly.” Self-directed forms include “take it on oneself,” as in Xuansha's words, “You just lack taking it on yourself,” and “setting the mind is only a matter of taking it on yourself.” A record asks, “What is the phrase of taking it on?” The negative form means inability to take it on: “Since you cannot take it on, I use expedients to urge you.” A nearby verb means “to shoulder” and appears alongside it. The records thus describe receiving, bearing, or assuming something directly; this entry does not infer an unstated object or contrast.
Senses.Note: This corpus-wide verb is not confined to one master's idiom. The curated passages span Xuansha Shibei, Yuanwu Keqin, and lamp-record exchanges. The negative line belongs to a multi-speaker exchange, so its speaker field remains null. Compare “to shoulder.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 本體不動佛。只欠自承當。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Xuansha Shibei's Extensive Record: Xuansha says, “You just lack taking it on yourself.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 是諸佛頂族。汝既承當不得。所以我方便勸汝。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 景德傳燈錄, Xuansha Shibei section. Xuansha Shibei is the exact teaching-seat speaker who tells the assembly that because they cannot take it on, he uses expedients to urge them. The full context remains within Xuansha's uninterrupted address; the section heading, book and TEI titles, and parallel contextual checks confirm Xuansha rather than leaving the speaker unnamed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 見人當面，不自承當，方便撥正，
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Essentials of the Mind by Foguo Keqin: Yuanwu describes someone who does not take it on himself and an old worthy who uses expedients to set him straight.

Occurrences.Kwic: 各得恰合，直下承當。如何是承當一句？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: 空谷道澄禪師語錄. Konggu Daocheng is the exact actor: his discourse says 直下承當 and asks 如何是承當一句.
